entries.name: Investopedia
entries.description: Investopedia.com is a website that provides educational content, news, analysis, and tools related to investing, finance, and business.

entries.name: Investor.gov

entries.name: WallStreetMojo
entries.description: Free finance tutorials with more than 10,000 articles on investment banking, financial modeling, valuation, and Excel.

entries.name: Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits
entries.description: Philip A. Fisher, 1958 This book is considered a classic of growth investing. Fisher, who taught investment courses at Stanford Graduate School of Business, explains his basic views and his approach to selecting stocks.

entries.name: Damodaran on Valuation: Security Analysis for Investment and Corporate Finance
entries.description: Aswath Damodaran, 1994 Damodaran explains aspects of valuation, from the basics of estimating cash flows and discount rates to the principles for using multiples.

entries.name: Margin of Safety: Risk-Averse Value Investing Strategies for the Thoughtful Investor
entries.description: Seth Klarman, 1991 Margin of Safety explains the key fundamentals and practices of value investing. Klarman outlines what value investing looks like and where investors might find attractive opportunities.

entries.name: Security Analysis
entries.description: Benjamin Graham, David L. Dodd, 1934 This book laid the intellectual foundation for what would later be called value investing. The first edition was published in 1934, shortly after the Wall Street crash and start of the Great Depression.

entries.name: The Alchemy of Finance
entries.description: George Soros, 1987 This book offers insight into the decision-making process of one of the most successful wealth managers, George Soros.

entries.name: The Dhandho Investor: The Low-Risk Value Method to High Returns
entries.description: Mohnish Pabrai, 2007 Written by Mohnish Pabrai, an investor of Indian origin, the book explains his value investing approach using the Dhandho capital allocation framework.

entries.name: The Intelligent Investor
entries.description: Benjamin Graham, 1949 In this book, Graham explains his investment principles and views regarding an investor's mindset. He shows how investors analyze the actual performance of companies and advises to disregard the changing moods of the market.

entries.name: The Little Book of Value Investing
entries.description: Christopher H. Browne, 2006 Browne explains the basic approaches of the value investing philosophy, but without making any big promises about market success. He provides guidance on the use of simple metrics such as the price-earnings ratio.

entries.name: The Most Important Thing
entries.description: Howard Marks, 2011 In this book, Howard Marks summarizes investment insights from his client memos and explains his investment philosophy.

entries.name: The Thoughtful Investor
entries.description: Basant Maheshwari, 2014 Maheshwari, a renowned Indian investor, explains in his book topics of financial analysis, the analysis of individual sectors and the behavioral aspect of investing.

entries.name: The Warren Buffett Way
entries.description: Robert G. Hagstrom, 1994 The book describes the business and investment principles of value investing according to Warren Buffett.

entries.name: Value Investing: From Graham to Buffett and Beyond
entries.description: Bruce C. N. Greenwald, Judd Kahn, Paul D. Sonkin, Michael van Biema, 2001 Greenwald explains the basic techniques of value investing and, in this context, illustrates their application using profiles of successful investors.

entries.name: Active Portfolio Management
entries.description: Richard C. Grinold, Ronald N. Kahn, 1995 In this book, Grinold and Kahn show how economics, econometrics, and operations research can be used to solve practical investment problems and identify profit opportunities.

entries.name: Portfolio Selection: Efficient Diversification of Investments
entries.description: Harry M. Markowitz, 1959 A comprehensive explanation of analysis and calculation methods to help investors find the best combinations of securities to match their requirements.

entries.name: Quantitative Equity Portfolio Management
entries.description: Ludwig B. Chincarini, Daehwan Kim, 2006 The authors address the construction and management of a portfolio using quantitative methods. Among other things, they offer explanations of factor models and the prediction of premiums and exposures.

entries.name: A Random Walk Down Wall Street
entries.description: Burton G. Malkiel, 1973 Malkiel argues that stock prices largely reflect available information and that most investors are better served by low-cost index funds than by stock picking or market timing. The book is a standard reference for the efficient market hypothesis and passive investing.

entries.name: Beating the Street
entries.description: Peter Lynch, John Rothchild, 1993 In the book, Lynch, a successful fund manager from 1977 to 1990, gives readers insight into his investment methods and tactics.

entries.name: Charlie Munger: The Complete Investor
entries.description: Tren Griffin, 2015 Tren Griffin uses interviews, writings, and letters to explain the investment philosophy and thought processes of Charlie Munger, the late vice chairman of Berkshire Hathaway and longtime business partner of Warren Buffett.

entries.name: Market Wizards: Interviews with Top Traders
entries.description: Jack D. Schwager, 1989 By interviewing successful investors such as Bruce Kovner, Richard Dennis, Paul Tudor Jones, Michael Steinhardt, Ed Seykota, Marty Schwartz, Tom Baldwin, and others, Schwager explores what separates the world's best traders from the vast majority of unsuccessful investors.

entries.name: One Up On Wall Street
entries.description: Peter Lynch, John Rothchild, 1989 Peter Lynch, who managed Fidelity Investments' successful Magellan Fund from 1977 to 1990, gives investors an insight into his investment methods. Using simple examples and some practices, he explains his process of stock selection.

entries.name: Reminiscences of a Stock Operator
entries.description: Edwin Lefèvre, 1923 A thinly fictionalized account of speculator Jesse Livermore's career, describing how he read the tape, followed trends, and managed risk. Generations of traders regard it as the classic text on speculation and trader psychology.

entries.name: Stocks for the Long Run
entries.description: Jeremy Siegel, 1994 The book by Siegel, a finance professor, addresses how to build a balanced portfolio and explains how investors can avoid typical mistakes.

entries.name: The Battle for Investment Survival
entries.description: Gerald M. Loeb, 1935 Now more than 90 years old, Gerald M. Loeb's work is considered a classic of financial literature. In his explanations, Loeb straightforwardly explains how investors should behave in rising and falling markets.

entries.name: The Complete TurtleTrader
entries.description: Michael W. Covel, 2007 The author tells the story of Richard Dennis, a highly successful commodities trader of the 1980s, and how he turned a group of beginners, under his guidance, into extraordinarily successful traders.

entries.name: The Craft of Investing
entries.description: John Train, 1994 In the book, Train outlines his key strategies and principles that have brought him success, addressing everything from the psychology of the market to practical portfolio management tips.

entries.name: The Little Book of Trading
entries.description: Michael W. Covel, 2011 Michael W. Covel's book offers insights into the rules and philosophies used by successful traders. Drawing on the author's own trading experience and the wisdom of other traders, the book offers advice in a direct and easy-to-understand manner.

entries.name: The Little Book that Still Beats the Market
entries.description: Joel Greenblatt, 2010 Joel Greenblatt explains how investors can outperform the popular market averages by systematically applying a formula. The book is kept simple and is aimed at beginners.

entries.name: The New Market Wizards
entries.description: Jack D. Schwager, 1992 Jack Schwager interviews some of the most successful traders in the United States. Through these interviews, Schwager offers insight into the strategies, perspectives, and psychological insights of successful traders.

entries.name: Trade Like a Stock Market Wizard
entries.description: Mark Minervini, 2013 Minervini presents his SEPA (Specific Entry Point Analysis) method for finding growth stocks before large price moves. The book covers stock selection, timing entries with chart patterns, and strict risk management to protect capital.

entries.name: Following the Trend
entries.description: Andreas F. Clenow, 2012 Clenow, a hedge fund manager, explains diversified trend following across futures markets in enough detail for readers to build their own strategy. He argues that position sizing and risk management matter more than entry and exit rules, and shows how such a strategy performed year by year.

entries.name: Investing with Volume Analysis
entries.description: Buff Dormeier, 2011 Dormeier offers insights into using volume metrics to enhance stock trading strategies, providing a framework for interpreting price-volume relationships to predict market trends.

entries.name: Trend Following
entries.description: Michael W. Covel, 2004 Michael W. Covel's book explains trend following without explicitly addressing specific strategies and provides insights on how to use trend following in market situations, whether bull or bear markets.

entries.name: Trend Qualification and Trading
entries.description: L. A. Little, 2011 Through a proven technical approach, the book explains how to gauge the likelihood of trend continuation and its potential for better trading results. Readers will gain an understanding of timing entries, taking profits, and effectively exiting trades based on these trends.

entries.name: Trend Trading Set-Ups
entries.description: L. A. Little, 2012 Building on the neoclassical concept, Little presents traders and investors with a robust methodology to discover promising trade setups and achieve precise timing for trade entry.

entries.name: Pring on Price Patterns
entries.description: Martin J. Pring, 2004 Martin J. Pring's book provides a comprehensive examination of the most commonly used price patterns and offers insights into their effectiveness and logic. The book covers a range of patterns, including one- and two-bar patterns, outside bars, reversals, pennants, and more.

entries.name: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets
entries.description: John J. Murphy, 1999 Murphy's standard reference covers chart construction, trends, price patterns, moving averages, oscillators, and intermarket analysis. It is widely used as a core text for learning technical analysis.

entries.name: Trading Price Action Trends
entries.description: Al Brooks, 2011 Al Brooks' book is intended as a practical guide to profiting from institutional trading trends. The book breaks down Brooks' trading system into its essential components such as institutional piggybacking or trend trading.

entries.name: Irrational Exuberance
entries.description: Robert J. Shiller, 2000 Robert J. Shiller's book addresses the psychological and behavioral factors that influence financial markets. It explores the concept of speculative bubbles and irrational exuberance, in which exuberant investor behavior leads to overvaluation of assets.
section: Behavioral Finance and Psychological Aspect of Investing

entries.name: The Little Book of Behavioral Investing: How Not to Be Your Own Worst Enemy
entries.description: James Montier, 2010 Author James Montier looks at the psychological aspects of investing and examines common behavioral biases that can hinder investors' success in the marketplace.
section: Behavioral Finance and Psychological Aspect of Investing

entries.name: The Wisdom of Crowds
entries.description: James Surowiecki, 2004 James Surowiecki's book addresses the concept that large groups of people collectively have higher intelligence than individual experts. Surowiecki supports his argument with various case studies and anecdotes from different fields.
section: Behavioral Finance and Psychological Aspect of Investing

entries.name: Thinking, Fast and Slow
entries.description: Daniel Kahneman, 2011 Nobel laureate Kahneman describes the two systems of thinking behind human judgment and the biases they produce, such as overconfidence, anchoring, and loss aversion. It is a foundational text for behavioral finance.
section: Behavioral Finance and Psychological Aspect of Investing

entries.name: Against the Gods
entries.description: Peter L. Bernstein, 1996 Bernstein takes the reader on a journey through time, showing how societies throughout history have dealt with uncertainty and developed methods for measuring and managing risk. The author shows the profound impact of risk and probability on human decision making and the development of modern finance.

entries.name: Fooled by Randomness
entries.description: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, 2001 Part of Taleb's multi-volume philosophical essay on uncertainty, this book examines various misconceptions of chance, including survivorship bias and skewed distributions, and illuminates how people tend to seek explanations even when there are none.

entries.name: The 5 Mistakes Every Investor Makes and How to Avoid Them
entries.description: Peter Mallouk, 2014 Mallouk's work discusses the most common mistakes investors make and how to avoid them. Among the most important lessons are the pitfalls of market timing and active trading, which are suboptimal compared to passive strategies.

entries.name: The Black Swan
entries.description: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, 2007 Taleb explores the concept of so-called black swans. These are rare and unpredictable events that have massive consequences and are often rationalized retroactively.

entries.name: Dot.con: How America Lost Its Mind and Money in the Internet Era
entries.description: John Cassidy, 2002 Cassidy chronicles the rise and fall of the dot-com bubble with insight and flair. He introduces the key players and events that shaped the Internet era, from visionary entrepreneurs to ruthless investors.

entries.name: The Big Short
entries.description: Michael Lewis, 2010 Lewis follows the small group of investors who recognized the US housing bubble and bet against subprime mortgage bonds before the 2008 financial crisis. The book shows how the crisis built up inside the financial system.

entries.name: When Genius Failed
entries.description: Roger Lowenstein, 2000 Lowenstein tells the story of Long-Term Capital Management, the hedge fund whose highly leveraged bets collapsed in 1998 and forced a Federal Reserve-organized rescue. It is a classic case study in leverage, model risk, and liquidity.

entries.name: Australian Securities Exchange (ASX)
entries.description: Primary securities exchange in Australia. Strong concentration in mining, commodities, and financial services.

entries.name: B3 (Brasil, Bolsa, Balcão)
entries.description: The main exchange in Brazil and Latin America. Operates equities, derivatives, and clearing services.

entries.name: BSE (formerly Bombay Stock Exchange)
entries.description: Asia’s oldest stock exchange. Major venue for Indian equities and indices.

entries.name: Deutsche Börse Frankfurt
entries.description: Germany’s principal stock exchange (formerly Börse Frankfurt), operated by Deutsche Börse. Electronic trading is conducted via Deutsche Börse Xetra.

entries.name: Euronext
entries.description: Pan-European exchange group operating regulated markets in multiple European countries, including France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Ireland, Portugal, Italy, Norway, and Greece.

entries.name: Hong Kong Stock Exchange (HKEX)
entries.description: Key international financial hub connecting Chinese and global capital markets.

entries.name: Korea Exchange (KRX)
entries.description: South Korea’s sole securities exchange operator, covering equities, derivatives, and bonds.

entries.name: London Stock Exchange (LSE)
entries.description: One of the world’s leading international listing venues, particularly for global and cross-border issuers.

entries.name: NASDAQ
entries.description: Electronic exchange with a strong focus on technology and growth-oriented companies.

entries.name: National Stock Exchange of India (NSE)
entries.description: India’s largest exchange by trading volume, known for its fully electronic infrastructure.

entries.name: New York Stock Exchange (NYSE)
entries.description: Central venue for large-cap and blue-chip companies, operating a hybrid trading model.

entries.name: Saudi Exchange (Tadawul)
entries.description: The main equity market of Saudi Arabia and the Gulf region, operated by Saudi Tadawul Group. Strong weighting in energy, petrochemicals, and banking.

entries.name: Shanghai Stock Exchange (SSE)
entries.description: Major mainland Chinese exchange, focused on large state-owned and industrial enterprises.

entries.name: Shenzhen Stock Exchange (SZSE)
entries.description: Chinese exchange with emphasis on growth, technology, and small- to mid-cap companies.

entries.name: Singapore Exchange (SGX)
entries.description: Regional financial hub with strengths in derivatives, commodities, and international listings.

entries.name: SIX Swiss Exchange
entries.description: Switzerland’s principal exchange, known for stability and strong representation of financial and life-science firms.

entries.name: Taiwan Stock Exchange (TWSE)
entries.description: Taiwan's principal securities exchange. Strong concentration in semiconductors and the electronics supply chain.

entries.name: Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE)
entries.description: Japan’s primary exchange, operated by Japan Exchange Group (JPX).

entries.name: Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX)
entries.description: Canada’s main equity market, globally relevant for mining and energy companies.
